abstract: Stem cells faithfully generate tissue architecture during development, yet how their identity and regenerative output are reshaped as anatomical niches mature and environmental signals change with aging and injury remains poorly understood. Rare skeletal stem cells (SSCs) across diverse skeletal sites are defined by combinations of cell-surface markers, precluding their genetic interrogation in vivo. Here, using spatially informed single cell transcriptomics, we identify Pannexin-3 (Panx3) to mark a dynamic functional state within bona fide SSCs and establish Panx3-CreERT2 mice for its longitudinal interrogation. Panx3 SSCs exhibit long-term clonal persistence, self-renewal and multipotency, whereas Panx3- SSCs can acquire this state. Successive SSC cohorts engage the Panx3 state during skeletal development, osteoanabolic stimulation expands pre-existing Panx3 SSC clones and injury induces it locally in previously unlabeled progenitors. Thus, anatomically distinct progenitors can converge on a common stem cell state in response to different environmental inputs. Three-dimensional reconstruction of chondrogenic niches further identifies signals that redirect Panx3-lineage cells towards stable cartilage, enabling durable regeneration in aged and osteoarthritic joints and with human SSCs. These findings establish anatomical origin, stem cell state and lineage fate as separable dimensions of stem cell identity and provide genetic access for interrogating and directing endogenous SSC function.
